description: Clew Labs is a civic-tech builder who turns dense information into plain, friendly tools. For Space Apps 2026 we're building Ghost Rovers: an interactive Moon map where the hardware NASA left behind tells kids its own story, using NASA's NSSDCA catalog. Small team, virtual, LA event. Welcome: storytellers, illustrators, and front-end folks who care about accuracy and accessibility.
summary: Ghost Rovers is a 1969 Mission Control console where kids ages 8 to 12 call the 12 machines NASA left on the Moon and Mars. Pick a machine, press CALL GHOST, and see who answers: 5 Moon machines stay quiet, the Apollo 11 Laser Mirror still answers, and all 6 on Mars are silent. Yet. It turns NASA's catalog records, which read like a spec sheet, into stories a kid can play with, so the hardware we left behind is not forgotten. Every fact comes from NASA records, maps and photos, checked by a human.
details:
What it does

Ghost Rovers is a free web app for kids ages 8 to 12, and the teachers and parents next to them. No login, no download. You sit at a 1969 Mission Control console with two worlds to explore: a 3D Moon and a 3D Mars you can spin, each wrapped in NASA's own map. Twelve machines NASA left behind are out there, 6 on each world.

On the Moon: Surveyor 3, the Apollo 11 Laser Mirror, Eagle's launch pad, the Apollo 12 moonquake station, and the Apollo 15 and 17 rovers. Pick one and press CALL GHOST. Radio static. Five answer NO SIGNAL with the year they went quiet. One answers: the Apollo 11 Laser Mirror. You watch a laser leave Earth, hit the Moon and come back in 2.5 seconds, because scientists still bounce lasers off it today.

On Mars: press M and the console flips to Viking 1 and 2, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity and InSight. Call them and none of them answer. They have gone quiet for good, and no person has ever visited them. Yet. But Mars is not silent: finish the Mars check and the console points you to the 2 rovers that still answer Earth today, Curiosity (Gale Crater, since 2012) and Perseverance (Jezero Crater, since 2021).

Every machine has a file: its original mission, a short story in its own voice, 3 questions kids actually ask ("Could I drive it?" "What's it made of?"), its real NASA photo, and a live counter of how long it has been sitting there, down to the second. READ TO ME reads the file out loud. Check all 6 on a world and you earn a Junior Flight Controller badge.

A full study kit for classrooms

Ghost Rovers comes with a free, public study notebook built in Gemini Notebook (NotebookLM) from the same NASA sources the app uses:

  • A quiz for the Moon and a quiz for Mars
  • Flashcards for each world
  • A mind map for each world
  • A podcast about the Moon ghosts (AI voices, labeled as AI)

When kids finish all 6 ghosts, the console hands them that world's quiz, flashcards and mind map. Teachers get a note in the ABOUT panel and the whole kit in one link.

Accurate, not just fun

All 12 ghosts were checked line by line against NASA's NSSDCA records, and the check caught real overclaims. "The first car on the Moon" became "the first car astronauts drove on the Moon," because a Soviet robot rover got there first in 1970. Both fact-check logs are public: Moon and Mars.

Built for every kid

  • WCAG 2.1 AA from day one, with 0 axe-core violations on both worlds
  • Full keyboard play: 1 to 6 picks, C calls, M flips worlds
  • Screen reader labels and calm announcements for every call
  • 44 px tap targets, and no spinning or beams when reduced motion is on
  • Fits phones, tablets and laptops without scrolling
  • No accounts, no tracking, no data collected

Why it's different

Most projects show you the hardware. Ghost Rovers lets you call it. The 1969 console is period-accurate down to the Dymo tape labels, the amber clocks and the console sounds, which are generated in code, not recorded. One machine answering out of 12 makes kids care about the other 11.

How it was built

Plain HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript ES modules, Three.js for the Moon and Mars globes wrapped in NASA's own maps, hosted on GitHub Pages. No framework, no server, no build step. Two JSON files hold every fact, one per world.

I directed the build in small blocks: each one was proposed, approved by me, built, then independently checked (screenshots at 3 screen sizes, an accessibility scan and a live test) before the next block started. Every use of SI is labeled in the project and logged in AI_DISCLOSURE.md.

What's next

  • Mission Control voice clips, recorded by a human
  • Ghost names with personality
  • A Spanish version
